title: Kongo spiritualities: objects and change
question: How can we study spiritual practices without reducing them to a single religion?
standfirst: Minkisi, ritual specialists and Kongo Christianities illuminate relations with power, protection and the spiritual world. Surviving objects do not encompass every practice.

thesis.heading: A turning point, not a uniform replacement

figures.claim: Nzinga Nkuwu is baptised and takes the name João.
figures.provenance: A royal event; it does not describe every inhabitant’s belief.

chapters.title: Minkisi and community
chapters.question: What does a ritual object do?
chapters.standfirst: A figure’s meaning also depends on its uses.

body.text: A nkisi, plural minkisi, connects material form with ritual power. The Mangaaka entry describes collaboration between a sculptor and a nganga, the specialist involved in its activation.
This Mangaaka, dated around 1880–1900, helps protect the community and settle commitments. Its metal pieces record interventions rather than merely decorating the figure.

readings.label: A documented social role
readings.body: The entry connects the figure to oaths and agreements. Spiritual practice and the regulation of social relations meet in this use.

readings.label: One figure cannot encompass a world
readings.body: Almeida distinguishes several forces, practices and mediators. Reading one object as a summary of all beliefs would generalise beyond it.

illustration.alt: Standing Mangaaka figure, hands on hips, with metal pieces covering its torso.
illustration.caption: Mangaaka, around 1880–1900, Chiloango region. A ritual figure associated with community protection.

chapters.title: Kongo Christianities
chapters.question: What happens to a religion as it travels?

body.text: Almeida describes Christian rites spreading unevenly across places and social positions. Royal baptism does not establish a collective, immediate abandonment of earlier practices.
Fromont also describes multilingual Kongo participants learning, translating and discussing doctrine. Religious history involves their intellectual work and political ambitions.

readings.label: Material evidence
readings.body: The Met crucifix reworks a Christian model in a Kongo visual language. Its forms testify to local meaning-making.

readings.label: Atlantic connections
readings.body: Fromont follows these references beyond Central Africa. This historical connection cannot establish a person’s religion from their origin.

illustration.alt: Brass crucifix with a central Christ and several smaller figures.
illustration.caption: Kongo crucifix, sixteenth–seventeenth century. A local reinterpretation, not a royal portrait.

gaps.reason: This dossier concerns documented historical practices. It offers neither a complete pantheon, a measure of present beliefs, nor a general equivalence with vodun.
